title: Why compressed files sometimes get bigger
description: Some files genuinely cannot be made smaller. Reporting that accurately is harder than reporting a fake percentage — and far more useful.
seoDescription: Why honest file-size reporting matters: what happens when compression makes a file bigger, and why saying so is more useful than a flattering number.

body.text: Try compressing a file that is already optimally compressed. Nothing happens. The bytes are already arranged as well as the format allows, so any re-encode is a fresh encoding of the same picture — and a fresh encoding is very often slightly larger than the one you already had.
A percentage alone can be confusing here. Compare both byte counts and look for an explicit description of whether the output is smaller, unchanged or larger.

body.caption: Three outcomes. Only the first is a saving, and it is the only one worth celebrating.

body.text: Every result here is described in the same line, with both real sizes and a percentage, because a percentage alone hides the absolute numbers. What changes is the wording:

items: Genuinely smaller — "12.40 MB → 4.80 MB · 61% smaller". A real saving, stated plainly.
The same size — "1.30 KB → 1.30 KB · no size change". Not a failure, but not a win either, and worth saying.
Larger — "828 B → 847 B · 2% larger than the original", plus a sentence explaining whether that is expected.

body.text: The distinction that matters: compressor or converter

A file coming out larger is not always bad news. It depends entirely on what the tool was asked to do. An image compressor that returns a bigger file is telling you the original was already efficient. A converter that rasterises a vector into a bitmap is supposed to return a bigger file — you asked for a different format, and a different format has a different size.

Conflating those two cases is how you end up with a tool that claims your PDF-to-images conversion "failed to compress". It did not fail. It did what you asked, and the honest description depends on which job it was doing.

body.title: The rule
body.text: Never present growth as a saving. If the output is larger, say it is larger, and say whether that was expected.
What this is worth to you

A number you can trust is worth more than a number that flatters the tool. If every result reads 60% smaller regardless of input, then the one time you need the real answer — the file that is already optimal — you have no way to get it.
